newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain knows role in NATO tied to place in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Spain knows role in NATO tied to place in Europe.

text.p: Spain's leaders are preparing to host a historic NATO summit mindful that playing a full role in the military alliance is inextricably linked to securing a place among the countries steering Europe into the future.

The July 8-9 summit on expanding NATO, to be attended by up to 44 heads of state, will provide a stage for Spain to demonstrate its eagerness to put isolationism firmly behind and help shape European and international affairs.

After the country joined 15 years ago, opposition Socialists fought an election campaign under the slogan "No to NATO entry". Following their victory they reversed the policy when they realised the doors to the European community would not swing open so easily if they pulled out.
In its first year in power, the current centre-right government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar has also made integration into Europe its top priority.
"With this summit, Madrid will obtain a very high international profile," Defence Minister Eduardo Serra told Reuters in an interview. "The new Spain is opening its doors to the world."
The successes of its economic austerity programme will make it hard to deny Spain a spot among the founders of a single European currency, scheduled to be launched in 1999.
At the same time, Aznar has asked for and received backing from parliament for full integration into NATO's military command.
"We are not a great power. But we don't like to be left behind if we can keep pace with the group in front," said chief Foreign Ministry spokesman Inocencio Arias.

NATO foreign ministers backed a bid by Spain to host the summit, during which the 16-member alliance will admit for the first time several eastern European countries once allied with the former Soviet Union.
The announcement of the venue came several weeks after Spanish parliament voted to participate in NATO's military structure last November.

Some diplomats in Madrid saw it as a pat on the back to Spain for breaking ranks with France, which continues to resist full integration. Paris and Washington are at loggerheads over American control of NATO's southern command, which France wants ceded to a European.
"We sympathise with the French position but we don't want to create any break with the United States," said Arias. "The alliance with the U.S. is very important."

Spain may also symbolise transition to democracy in the post-war era at a moment when the alliance incorporates former dictatorships. With the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975, Spain emerged from nearly 40 years of isolationism.
The contribution of NATO's Spanish Secretary-General Javier Solana may have made members sympathetic to Spain's request to host the summit.

Solana, a former Socialist foreign minister, was an outspoken critic of NATO in the early 1980s but then "converted". He made history on May 14 when he negotiated a landmark post-Cold War treaty between Russia and the Western allies.

Aznar may reaffirm Spain's willingness to join NATO's military structure during the summit. Serra said Madrid was satisfied that its key demands for integration had been met in negotiations with NATO.
Spain has insisted on an Iberian sub-regional command controlling all Spanish territory including the Canary islands and access to the Mediterranean via the Straits of Gibraltar.

Spain's embracing of NATO may seem surprising to some given its strong pacifist tradition. In the 1980s, Spanish citizens fiercely resisted joining NATO or stationing any nuclear weapons or American military bases on their soil.
That tradition will be kept alive on Saturday when Spain's opposition United Left coalition leads other European parties in an anti-NATO demonstration in Madrid.
